newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Old concern and fresh supply.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Old concern and fresh supply.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market has, once again, settled into a negative psychology with the 30-year bond likely to remain anchored around the 7.0 percent yield until the release of the August U.S. payrolls, analysts said on Monday.

"The psychology is negative and will remain so until next week. We'll be anchored around these levels until we see the employment report,"said MCM MoneyWatch, senior economist Astrid Adolfson, referring to the August payrolls data due out on September 6.
In late trade, the 6-3/4-percent 30-year bond was quoted down 18/32 to yield 7.00 percent -- backing up to that key psychological level for the first time since July 30.
"We are back to square one," added Adolfson who noted the early August market rebound started to fizzle after the release of the July Consumer Price Index.
"It started with the CPI data, up 0.3 percent, then with the weekly retail sales and jobless claims," Adolfson said.
High-frequency series such as weekly retail sales and jobless claims are pointing in the opposite direction of the Federal Reserve's bet on a second-half slowdown.
Such economic slowdown is seen as crucial for maintaining a steady monetary policy, with Fed officials reiterating their vigilance about inflation risks tied to above-trend growth.

One bond trader said the market is uneasy about the Fed's forecast. He added any sign the economy is not really slowing down is cause for concern and wide price swings, mainly in a market expected to remain thin until next week.

"People were assuming there was a real slowdown. We are slowing from the second quarter's 4.2 percent (Gross Domestic Product rise), but probably not very much," Adolfson noted. "The GDP is probably not falling below 2-1/4-percent growth."
Adolfson expected the payroll data to be -- once again -- the "make-or-break" report for the market.
"We'll remain around these levels until we see numbers that will convince us we need to go much higher (in terms of yields) or go back to our recent lows," Adolfson concluded.
An early consensus in a Reuter survey puts August payroll creation at 238,000, with a 5.3 percent unemployment rate and a 0.3-percent increase in the average hourly earnings.
If such forecast proves correct, it would draw the Fed closer to its first rate hike since February 1995. In July already, the Fed introduced a bias to tighten at any time.
Treasury's auctions of $18.75 billion in two-year notes and $12.5 billion in five-year notes will be held amid such negative psychology on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively.
Carol Stone, senior economist at Nomura Securities International, said the arrival of fresh supply at this juncture is "one of the reasons psychology is bad."

"Once we get beyond these two auctions this week, there might be some respite," said Stone who agreed with Adolfson the long bond yield will hover around 7.0 percent for the near term. "The market is going to be very apprehensive until the employment report."
The main economic release on Tuesday is The Conference Board's consumer confidence index for August. In a Reuter survey, it is forecast at 104.40 versus 107.2 in July.
On Monday, the Fed temporarily added reserves via three-day system repurchase agreements, supplementing a seven-day operation in place since last Thursday.
Federal funds are expected to open on target at 5.25 percent on Tuesday.
